edition: Issue #013 - A penalty shootout in Yokohama, a Fat Bear nepo-baby, and a Kiwi gaming billion
tagline: Your 3-minute break. Zero fluff, maximum banter.

stories.headline: All Whites settle the Kirin Cup semi on penalties - the sport's most expensive game of heads or tails
stories.summary: New Zealand beat Panama in a penalty shootout in Yokohama to reach the Kirin Cup final at Tokyo's National Stadium on Monday 5 October.

body.text: The All Whites are into the Kirin Cup final in Japan after beating Panama in a penalty shootout in Yokohama. Marko Stamenic opened the scoring after 13 minutes, and it looked like New Zealand would carry a 1-0 lead into the break until Panama's Giovany Herbert equalised just on halftime. Neither side found its rhythm in the second half, so it went to the spot. Five Kiwis - Tyler Bindon, Marko Stamenic, Moses Dyer, Lachlan Bayliss and Michael Boxall - held their nerve to secure the win. The final is at Tokyo National Stadium on Monday 5 October.

International football has a pretty good idea: put two nations through 90 minutes of running, sweating and small hopes, then decide the whole thing on who can kick a ball from 11 metres better at a goalkeeper who knows exactly where it is going. It is professional sport's most expensive game of heads or tails, and it is extremely unkind to anyone who sat through all the build-up. Still, credit where it is due: it took some nerve for five Kiwis to walk up to that spot in front of a Tokyo crowd, and they buried them. Easiest thing in the world to say, harder than it looks to actually do the walk from the halfway line without visibly sweating through your shorts.

RNZ (1 Oct 2026): The All Whites beat Panama in a penalty shootout (1-1 after 90 minutes) at International Stadium, Yokohama to advance to the Kirin Cup final. Marko Stamenic opened on 13 minutes; Giovany Herbert equalised for Panama just before halftime. The five successful Kiwi scorers were Tyler Bindon, Marko Stamenic, Moses Dyer, Lachlan Bayliss and Michael Boxall. New Zealand now plays the final at Tokyo National Stadium on Monday 5 October.

stories.headline: Fat Bear Week crowns a chop: nepo-baby bear Backpack wins Alaska's big eating contest
stories.summary: Backpack, the son of 2019 champion Holly, edged out Dancing Queen by 5,000 votes in the final to win the annual Fat Bear Week at Katmai National Park.

body.text: Alaska has crowned a new Fat Bear Week champion, and it is a family affair. Backpack - a 20-year-old male brown bear at Katmai National Park, known officially as Bear 89 - edged out fellow finalist Dancing Queen in the annual gorging contest that tracks how much weight brown bears pile on before hibernation. More than 2.3 million people voted over the week, and the final alone drew 200,000 votes that Backpack took by just 5,000. Rangers weighed him at about 544kg. His win follows that of his mother, Holly, who took the title in 2019; Backpack got his nickname for climbing on her back as she swam the river.

Hollywood has nepo babies, and apparently so does the Brooks River. Backpack did not just win Fat Bear Week, he inherited a legacy - his mother was champion in 2019, before he even started serious professional hibernating. It is the most wholesome nepotism on the planet, because the judges are cameramen, the prize is bragging rights, and the contestant in question is a 544-kilogram bear who once had a bad leg and adjusted his whole life to be lazy on rocks instead of fighting. The kid won by 5,000 votes out of 200,000 and it somehow felt like less of a landslide than we deserve. Vast, furry, allergic to effort, riding on a family name. We are fully behind it.

NZ Herald / AFP (2 Oct 2026): Fat Bear Week is an annual contest at Katmai National Park, Alaska, showing how much weight brown bears put on before hibernation. This year's winner was Backpack (officially Bear 89), a 20-year-old male brown bear, who beat finalist Dancing Queen by 5,000 votes in a 200,000-vote final; more than 2.3 million people voted across the week. Rangers told Alaska Public Media he weighs about 544kg. His mother Holly won the contest in 2019. He was nicknamed Backpack from climbing on his mother's back while she swam across the river.

stories.headline: New Zealand's video game industry quietly clocks its first 1 billion year - two years early
stories.summary: Preliminary NZGDA figures show Kiwi game developers passed 1 billion in revenue in the year to March 2026, up from $758.9 million, hitting a target set for 2028 two years ahead of schedule.

body.text: New Zealand's video game industry has cracked a billion dollars. Preliminary figures from the New Zealand Game Developers Association show the sector generated more than 1 billion in revenue in the year to March 2026, up from $758.9 million the year before - and two years ahead of the 2028 target the industry originally set itself. The sector is overwhelmingly export-focused, with 95 percent of its 2025 revenue coming from international consumer sales, and it employed 1,418 full-time equivalent workers. The milestone lands as the NZ Game Developers Conference returns to Auckland for the first time in nearly a decade, with the makers of the Roblox hit 99 Nights in the Forest among the stars - a game Disney-owned 20th Century Studios is turning into a film.

A small country on the edge of the map quietly makes a billion dollars a year building imaginary worlds, most of which are slurped up by people on the other side of the planet, and somehow this is the story that barely makes the front page. The industry keeps calling itself a weightless export, and it is the best kind: no cargo holds, no freight, no butter wars - just a few hundred people in Auckland and Dunedin making things people pay for on the other side of the world. And they were supposed to hit a billion in 2028. They were two years early. If the rest of the economy ran on that kind of ambition, the budget would balance itself before morning tea.

The Post / NZGDA (26 Sep 2026): Preliminary figures from the NZ Game Developers Association show the sector generated more than 1 billion in revenue in the year to March 2026, up from $758.9 million the previous year, reaching its target two years ahead of the original 2028 forecast. 95% of 2025 revenue came from international consumer sales; the sector employed 1,418 full-time equivalent workers in 2025. NZGDA executive director Joy Keene said the sector was growing at more than 20 times the global average. The NZ Game Developers Conference ran in Auckland 30 Sep - 3 Oct as part of Auckland Games Week.

affiliate_cta.headline: Planning a break, a nest, or a long winter of your own?
affiliate_cta.body: Whether you are training to hold your nerve from the spot, bulking up before a long winter (absolutely acceptable), or just levelling up your weekend with a good game, a couple of harmless starting points never went astray. No pressure, no commitment, and sadly no 544kg bears involved.
